nameStory: Seaside sandmat gets its name from its love of sandy coastal areas and its distinctive growth habit. This little spurge hugs the ground like a living mat, spreading its stems flat across beach sand and dunes. The 'seaside' part is obvious once you find it - this plant has made the challenging saltwater environment its specialty.
description: Seaside sandmat is a small, sprawling annual herb that forms flat mats on sandy beaches and coastal areas. This low-growing member of the spurge family rarely gets more than a few inches tall, instead spreading its smooth, reddish stems horizontally across the sand. Its tiny oval leaves are thick and waxy, perfectly adapted for life by the sea. Like all spurges, it produces a milky white sap when broken.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms distinctive flat mats with stems that lie completely prostrate against the sand, radiating outward from the center like wheel spokes

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves that feel thick and slightly waxy to the touch, often with a blue-green color and sometimes tinged reddish

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, often reddish or pinkish stems that are surprisingly sturdy despite being thin, lying flat against the ground

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous greenish flowers clustered at leaf joints - you'll need to look closely as they're easily missed

idTips.label: Sap
idTips.description: Breaks stems to reveal milky white latex sap, characteristic of all spurges - avoid getting this on skin as it can cause irritation

habitat: Look for seaside sandmat on sandy beaches, dunes, and coastal flats along New England's Atlantic shore. It thrives in the harsh conditions near salt water where few other plants can survive, often growing in pure sand with little organic matter. You'll typically find it in the upper beach zone, just beyond where the highest tides reach.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small green rosettes in late spring, beginning to spread their characteristic mat-like growth pattern across the sand.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when the prostrate mats are most visible and extensive, with tiny flowers appearing throughout the summer months.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to turn reddish or purplish as cooler weather arrives, making them actually more noticeable against the pale sand before they die back.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, leaving only seeds in the sand to sprout the following spring - no above-ground parts remain.

funFact: Seaside sandmat is one of the few plants tough enough to grow in pure beach sand with virtually no soil nutrients, surviving solely on what the ocean waves wash ashore and what its roots can extract from the harsh, salty environment.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small, mat-forming beach plants, but seaside sandmat's perfectly flat growth habit and milky sap when broken are distinctive. Remember: if it's not completely flat against the sand like a living carpet, it's probably not seaside sandmat.
contextualKnowledge: Like all spurges, seaside sandmat produces a milky latex sap that can cause skin and eye irritation in sensitive people, so it's best to observe rather than handle. Despite being in the same family as the popular holiday poinsettia, this humble beach plant couldn't look more different from its showy relative.
compareHints: Among New England's spurges, seaside sandmat is unique in its completely prostrate, mat-forming habit and coastal habitat. While spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat also grow low to the ground, they're found in disturbed inland areas rather than beaches. Seaside sandmat's thick, waxy leaves and ability to thrive in pure sand distinguish it from all other regional spurges, which prefer richer soils.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other spurges in New England that typically have broader, more conventional leaves, cypress spurge is instantly recognizable by its needle-like foliage.
Among New England's spurges, spotted spurge is unique for its ground-hugging mat formation and distinctly spotted leaves.
Among New England spurges, slender leafy spurge is distinguished by its tall, narrow growth form and lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's spurges, nodding spurge is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth and drooping flower clusters.
Unlike other New England spurges which are mostly weedy annuals with thin leaves, Donkey Tail is a perennial succulent with thick, fleshy foliage.
Among New England's sandmat spurges, Wormseed Sandmat is distinguished by its perfectly circular growth pattern and distinctively ridged seeds.
Among New England spurges, caper spurge is unique for its large size and architectural growth habit - most other spurges are low-growing weeds or small garden plants.
Unlike the tall, weedy leafy spurge or the ground-hugging spotted spurge, cushion spurge maintains a perfectly rounded, compact form.
Among New England spurges, petty spurge is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
Flowering spurge towers over most of its spurge relatives in New England, which tend to be low, mat-forming plants like spotted spurge or cypress spurge.
Snow-on-the-mountain is easily distinguished from other New England spurges by its distinctive white-margined leaves - most other spurges in our region have plain green foliage.

Leafy spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its tall, upright growth and dense leafy appearance - most of its relatives like spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat are low, sprawling plants.
Among New England spurges, graceful spurge stands out for its relatively tall, upright growth compared to the ground-hugging spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat.
Among New England's spurges, thymeleaf sandmat is distinguished by its ground-hugging mat formation and tiny thyme-like leaves.
Sweet spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its clumping perennial growth habit and relatively large, oval leaves.
Among New England spurges, green poinsettia stands out for its distinctly hairy, toothed leaves - most other spurges have smooth or nearly smooth leaves.
Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the spotted stems of spotted spurge, David's spurge has broader, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs.
Unlike other New England spurges that have broader, more typical-looking leaves, grassleaf spurge's ultra-narrow foliage makes it unique in the region.
Among New England's spurges, prostrate sandmat is uniquely flat-growing - most other spurges like cypress spurge or flowering spurge grow upright.
Unlike cypress spurge with its needle-like leaves or spotted spurge that grows as a low mat, eggleaf spurge stands upright with distinctly oval, toothed leaves.
Compared to other New England spurges, Florida hammock sandmat is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and extremely low, tight mat-forming habit.
Matted sandmat is flatter and more perfectly mat-forming than most other spurges in our region.
Among New England's spurges, ribseed sandmat is distinguished by its extremely rare occurrence and the ribbed seeds that give it its name.
